guest.bio_context: Madeline Schwartz is a reporter based in Paris. She grew up between New York and Paris, attending school in both cities, with an American mother and a French father who separated when she was a baby. This bicultural upbringing gives her firsthand experience of both French and American parenting cultures, which she draws on extensively in her reporting on this debate.

context.transcript_excerpt: From New York Times, I'm Michael Bavaro. This is The Daily on Sunday. In France, the question of how best to raise children has long seemed like a settled matter. After all, the country's reputation for strict parenting is revered for its results. Well-behaved children who, from toddlerdom, clean their plates right down to the strong, smelly cheese. But a new generation of French parents are questioning those methods, adopting a gentler, more American approach, and igniting a fierce national debate that has both sides accusing the other of being harmful to kids. Today, my conversation with reporter Madeline Schwartz on why this subject has become so divisive in France, and what it tells us about the eternal search for the right way to raise children. It's Sunday, August 9th. Madeline Schwartz, welcome to the Sunday Daily. Hi, it's nice to be here. So you are based in Paris, and from what I understand, this is a subject, the one we're going to be talking about, that is very close to you, because you yourself were raised in both the United States and there in France. Yeah, so my mom is American and my dad is French. They split up when I was just a baby, and so I grew up going between both New York and Paris, and went to school in both places. Well, I would argue that that makes you the ideal guest for this conversation that we're about to have about French versus American style parenting, because you've experienced both of these cultures in a pretty meaningful way. Yeah, well, I've certainly seen a lot. I'm sure you have. Okay, I'm curious, when were you first made aware of this kind of fierce debate in France about parenting? Yeah, so a few years ago, a woman named Caroline Goldman started appearing everywhere in French media. She's a psychologist, and she was being interviewed in Le Monde. She was writing op-eds and she was on television. It really seemed like she had become an inescapable figure of the zeitgeist. And she's a very charismatic, very media-friendly person who also carries with her a certain amount of mystique, in large part because her father is a very famous pop star named Jean-Jacques Goldman, who I don't know who the right analogy would be, but it's sort of like Francis Bruce Springsteen. He's a very, very beloved celebrity who has retreated from the public eye. And so anytime she would talk, people would really get very excited to hear from her and start trying to kind of analyze what she was saying. And what was she saying? Every appearance she had, had a very clear point, which is that she felt that children were being in many ways misled by their parents, that what we might know in the United States as gentle parenting had essentially led a generation of French children astray, and that it was time to go back to a more disciplinary form of education. So, this is quite surprising, because we here in the U.S. tend to think about French parenting as quite rule-bound, and the word gentle is not the one I would apply to that tradition. Well, for a very long time, French parenting has been very rule-bound and very defined by specific rules that children must follow in order to be integrated into society. And I think that a lot of Americans who know about French parenting do so because of a book called Bringing Up Baby, which was published in 2012 by Pamela Druckerman, who herself is an American journalist who moved to France and had three kids here, and has been a huge bestseller since. Right. I read this book even before I had children. It was just a mega thing here in the U.S. 10, 15 years ago. But for those who did not read it, just remind us what the book did. Yeah, so it's really an homage to French parenting. One of the things that I think made it so interesting to American parents is that it describes how you can have kids according to the French way and not have them take over your life. pending_qa.q: What role did Françoise Dolto play in shaping French parenting philosophy?
pending_qa.r: Françoise Dolto was a psychoanalyst who profoundly shaped generations of French parenting through her books and a popular radio program. She is credited with revolutionizing the concept of children's rights in France — championing the idea that children are people who can be spoken to as such — while simultaneously maintaining a very hierarchical, Catholic bourgeois worldview that reinforced France's rigid cultural rules and structures.
